metadata.chapter_title: BCM2_01_INU – Individual Utility (v3.0, compliant with Meta-Axioms)
metadata.context: This module represents the individual utility function. It implements Meta-Axioms 0.011–0.013 (Multi-dimensionality, Temporality, Context-dependence) as well as 0.041–0.042 (Time horizons and Uncertainty modulation) and 0.131 (Segment-specific weighting) from Module 7232. Thus, the individual utility function is defined as the first derivative of the meta-level. It integrates all relevant dimensions (FEPSDE) as well as mechanisms such as stress, social comparisons, technological disruptions, and ecological utility effects. This module forms the foundation of all individual analyses in BCM 2.0 and provides input for Awareness and Willingness processes. In every application, the WEIRD bias (Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, Democratic) must be explicitly considered to avoid misinterpretations due to cultural and institutional distortions.
scope: This module applies to all individual utility functions in BCM simulations.
It is applicable in WEIRD contexts (Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, Democratic) and in Non-WEIRD contexts (differing cultural, economic, and political frameworks).
It represents individual evaluations in the FEPSDE dimensions (financial, emotional, physical, social, digital, ecological).
It encompasses analyses along four time horizons (instant, short-, medium-, long-term) according to 7232 (0.041–0.042).
It is segment-specifically operationalizable (age, gender, socioeconomic status, life phases, culture) according to 7232 (0.131).
It supports intersectional segmentations.
It is the foundation for scenarios with stress, coping, social comparisons, disruptions, and ecological utility effects.
It serves as input for Awareness (7240) and Willingness functions (7243).
objectives: Representation of individual pain and gain structures in FEPSDE dimensions (financial, emotional, physical, social, digital, ecological) according to Meta-Axiom 0.011 (Multi-dimensionality).
Integration of temporal horizons (instant, short-, medium-, long-term) and their discounting according to Meta-Axiom 0.012 and 0.041–0.042.
Consideration of segment-specific differences (age, gender, socioeconomic status, life phase, culture) according to Meta-Axiom 0.131.
Representation of context-dependent effects on utility perception and weighting according to Meta-Axiom 0.013.
Integration of memory, learning, and dynamic adaptation of individual utility functions.
Consideration of cognitive biases, motivated beliefs, and blind spots.
Embedding of stress and coping mechanisms as well as resilience functions.
Representation of social comparison dynamics as influence on individual utility perception.
Representation of the effect of technological disruptions on individual utility functions.
Extension of the utility function with ecological dimensions and sustainability factors.
Provision of the interface to Awareness (7240) and Willingness function (7243) for behavioral implementation.
requirements: Pain and gain data in all FEPSDE dimensions (according to 0.011 Multi-dimensionality).
Explicit reference points for each dimension (individual, social, life-phase-dependent) according to 0.013.
Discounting parameters and time proxies (instant, short-, medium-, long-term) according to 0.012 and 0.041–0.042.
Uncertainty and risk parameters (φ_risk, φ_amb, φ_unc) according to 0.042.
Segment parameters: age, gender, socioeconomic status, life phase, culture, institutions according to 0.131.
Intersectional identity positions (combination of segment parameters).
Coping and resilience values for modeling stress effects.
Data on social comparison groups (peers, reference groups).
Ecological utility values (sustainability, resource usage, environmental impact).
Digital utility components (privacy, connectivity, reputation, identity).
boundaries: This module exclusively represents individual utility.
Collective utility (7235) and identity utility (7236) are separate modules and are not considered here.
External framework conditions (e.g., institutional structures, regulatory requirements) are only integrated insofar as they affect individual utility perceptions (Reference: 8904 KON, 9493 UNS_INS).
The aggregation of individual utility functions to group or societal utility occurs exclusively via 7235 (KNU).
The anchoring of individual utility functions in identities or affiliations occurs exclusively via 7236 (IDN).
This module is not responsible for deriving or operationalizing interventions – it provides input values for 9250 (INT).
versioning: v1.0 – Original version 7234: Introduction of individual utility function along FEPS dimensions with Pain/Gain separation.
v1.1 – Structural conformity according to 9232 (A1–A10 introduced).
v2.0 – Extension with gender, life phase, and culture dependencies; introduction of digital dimension.
v2.1 – Integration of intersectionality (combination of gender, age, SES, culture, institutions).
v2.2 – Extension with stress, coping, and resilience mechanisms.
v2.3 – Integration of social comparison dynamics.
v2.4 – Modeling of technological disruptions as utility shocks.
v2.5 – Introduction of ecological dimension (FEPSDE logic, sustainability).

v3.0 – Complete linkage to 7232 (Meta-Axioms: Multi-dimensionality, Temporality, Context, Time horizons, Segment logic), explicit consideration of WEIRD bias and clarification of module connections (A6).

axioms.title: Master Function of Individual Value Function
axioms.text: The individual value function V_individual of an action, activity, decision, behavior, or judgment results from the integration of multiple levels: (1) Baseline value of activity, (2) multidimensional gains and pains in FEPSDE, (3) reference points and loss aversion, (4) time dimension (instant, short-, medium-, long-term), (5) segment and context dependence, (6) dynamics through feedback, learning, and psychology, (7) collateral effects (Beauty & Damage), and (8) reaction time as measure of preference clarity. Thus, A0 represents the universal evaluation function that can be simulated for any individual action within BEATRIX.
axioms.formula: V_individual(a,t,k,s) = V_base(i) + Σ_{d∈FEPSDE} ω_d(t,s,k)[G_d(a,t) - λ_d(k,s) * P_d(a,t)] + C_intr,extr,idn(a,t,k,s) + CB(a,t,k,s) - CD(a,t,k,s) + RT_adj(a,t,k,s)

variables.s: Segment parameters (age, gender, socioeconomic status, life phase, etc.)
variables.V_base(i): Baseline value of activity for individual i
variables.ω_d(t,s,k): Weighting of dimension d depending on time, segment, and context
variables.λ_d(k,s): Loss aversion in dimension d, context- and segment-specific
variables.C_intr,extr,idn: Complementarity between intrinsic, extrinsic, and identity value
variables.CB(a,t,k,s): Collateral Beauty, positive unintended side effects
variables.CD(a,t,k,s): Collateral Damage, negative unintended side effects
variables.RT_adj(a,t,k,s): Reaction time adjustment, measures preference clarity

axioms.title: FEPSDE Structure
scope: This axiom applies to all individual value functions.
It represents the multi-dimensionality of individual value.
It is universally applicable in WEIRD and Non-WEIRD contexts.
It considers segment- and life-phase-dependent differences.
It is the foundation for integrating stress, social comparisons, and ecological utility effects.
axioms.text: Individual value results from six dimensions: financial, emotional, physiological, social, digital, ecological. Each dimension has a weight, gains and losses are represented separately, modified by loss aversion and context factors.
axioms.formula: N_ind(t) = Σ_{d∈{fin, emo, phy, soc, dig, eco}} ω_d(t) [G_d(t) - λ_d * P_d(t)]

axioms.title: Loss Aversion (Gain-Pain)
scope: This axiom applies to all dimensions of the FEPSDE structure.
It operationalizes the difference in weighting between gains and losses.
It enables context and segment specifications.
axioms.text: Losses are normally weighted more heavily than gains. The parameter λ can be greater than 1 (classical loss aversion), but also less than 1 (e.g., in masochism, asceticism, or athletic activities).

variables.λ_d: Loss aversion in dimension d, context-dependent

axioms.title: Baseline Value of Activity
scope: This axiom defines the basic value of human activity, behavior, decision-making, actions independent of specific tasks.
It forms the basis for distinguishing between intrinsic and extrinsic value.
It is segment-specific (e.g., age, culture, life phase).
axioms.text: Every activity has a basic value (V_base) that does not need to be explained by rewards or specific activities. It encompasses psychological, social, emotional, and physiological basic needs that are fulfilled through activity.

axioms.title: Intrinsic Value of Specific Activity
scope: This axiom models the utility that arises from the activity, behavior, action, decision-making itself.
It applies particularly strongly to psychological, social, emotional, and ecological dimensions.
It is independent of extrinsic rewards.
axioms.text: The intrinsic value of an activity results from experiencing the activity itself. Activities can be positively intrinsic (joy, flow, meaning) or negative (boredom, overwhelm).

axioms.title: Intrinsic Power Value
scope: This sub-axiom specifies the intrinsic value of specific activities (A4).
It applies to contexts where exercising power itself is a source of psychological utility.
It extends the emotional dimension (E) of the FEPSDE structure with an independent power term.
axioms.text: Individuals can derive utility from the mere exercise of power, even without instrumental benefits. This intrinsic power value reflects the psychological-emotional satisfaction from influence and control.

variables.U_Power_intr(t): Intrinsic utility of power exercise at time t
variables.WTP_Power(t): Observed willingness to pay for power exercise

axioms.title: Extrinsic Value of Specific Activity
scope: This axiom captures all external rewards tied to an activity, behavior, action, or decision.
It is particularly relevant for financial and reputation-based dimensions.
It interacts with intrinsic values (crowding-in / crowding-out).
axioms.text: Extrinsic value results from rewards or external factors (e.g., money, recognition, status, security). It can strengthen intrinsic motivation (complementarity) or weaken it (crowding-out).

axioms.title: Complementarity of Value Functions
scope: This axiom describes the interactions between baseline, intrinsic, and extrinsic values.
It applies universally to all activities, actions, and decisions.
It allows modeling of crowding-in and crowding-out effects.
axioms.text: The total value of an activity results not only from the addition of baseline, intrinsic, and extrinsic value, but also from their interactions. These can be complementary (mutual reinforcement) or substitutive (mutual weakening).
axioms.formula: V_total = V_base + V_intrinsic + V_extrinsic + κ(V_base, V_intrinsic, V_extrinsic)

axioms.title: Reference Points
scope: This axiom operationalizes the relative evaluation of utility and disutility.
It considers individual, social, and life-phase-dependent reference points.
It is context-dependent and segmentable.
axioms.text: Utility and disutility always arise relative to a reference point. This can be individual (e.g., income expectation), social (comparison with peers), or life-phase-dependent. If the reference point shifts, so does the evaluation.

variables.x_d(t): Actual outcome in dimension d at time t
variables.R_d(t): Individual reference point in dimension d

axioms.title: Time Evaluation
scope: This axiom models the temporal evaluation of utility and disutility.
It integrates different time horizons (instant, short-, medium-, long-term).
It allows both classical and hyperbolic discounting.
axioms.text: Utility is weighted differently depending on time horizon. Short-term gains and losses are often disproportionately salient, while medium- and long-term effects are more heavily discounted. This enables modeling of impatience, procrastination, and foresight.
axioms.formula: U_d(t) = Σ_{τ∈{inst, short, medium, long}} β_τ δ_τ^t U_{d,τ}(t)

variables.U_{d,τ}(t): Utility in dimension d for time horizon τ

axioms.title: Uncertainty & Risk
scope: This axiom describes the reduction of perceived value through risk, ambiguity, and uncertainty.
It applies universally to all FEPSDE dimensions.
It allows integration of individual risk preferences.
axioms.text: Individual evaluations are always associated with uncertainty. Risk (known probabilities), ambiguity (unknown probabilities), and uncertainty (incomplete knowledge) reduce perceived value. The effect varies in strength across dimensions.

axioms.title: Motivated Beliefs
scope: This axiom describes the distortion of beliefs to avoid disutility.
It applies universally and is particularly relevant for cognitive dissonance.
It is segment- and context-specifically operationalizable.
axioms.text: Individuals distort their beliefs when the truth would be too painful. This self-deception reduces short-term pain but can create long-term value losses. Motivated beliefs are a psychological protection mechanism.
axioms.formula: B^M_d(t) = B^R_d(t) * (1 - γ_d * max(0, P_d(t) - T_d))

variables.T_d: Threshold above which pain has distorting effect

axioms.title: Blind Spots
scope: This axiom describes the effect of filtered-out information on individual value.
It applies universally in all contexts.
It allows modeling of cognitive biases through conscious or unconscious information selection.
axioms.text: Individuals do not consider all available information but selectively filter out aspects. These blind spots reduce the perceived value of an action or increase it when critical information is ignored.

variables.φ_BS,d: Blind spot parameter in dimension d (0 ≤ φ ≤ 1)

axioms.title: Dynamic Adaptation
scope: This axiom models the ongoing adaptation of individual value functions.
It applies universally and allows simulation of learning processes.
It integrates feedback and context effects.
axioms.text: Individual value continuously adapts to external feedback and context influences. This dynamic is central to explaining learning processes and habituation effects.

axioms.title: Memory
scope: This axiom models the aftereffect of previous experiences on current value.
It applies universally in all dimensions.
It is segment- and context-dependent (e.g., age differences, cultural memory traditions).
axioms.text: Previous experiences affect current evaluation. The influence decreases exponentially over time but persists. This explains the persistence of habits and trauma.

variables.U_d(t-k): Value in dimension d k periods ago

axioms.title: Willingness Interface
scope: This axiom connects individual value with action readiness.
It operationalizes the transition from value to behavior.
It is strongly dependent on context and segment parameters.
axioms.text: Individual value is input for the decision whether an action is actually performed. This occurs through a threshold function that represents sensitivity to context factors.

axioms.title: Salience
scope: This axiom describes the perceptibility (salience) of different time horizons.
It applies universally but depends on awareness.
It explains why short-term utility and disutility dominate.
axioms.text: Immediate gains or losses are always salient, while medium- and long-term effects are only salient when activated by awareness. This axiom explains the tendency toward short-term thinking.

variables.Salience_{d,τ}(t): Salience in dimension d for time horizon τ

axioms.title: Life Phase Dependence
scope: This axiom describes the dependence of individual value on a person's life phase.
It considers biological, psychological, and social changes across the lifespan.
It allows modeling of heterogeneity between age cohorts.
axioms.text: The individual value of activities and decisions strongly depends on life phase. Needs, preferences, and sensitivities change along the life course. What has high value in youth may be irrelevant or negative in old age.

variables.U_d(t): Utility in dimension d at time t
variables.LCP_phase(t): Life phase parameter (childhood, youth, working phase, old age)

axioms.title: Gender Differentiation
scope: This axiom describes differences in individual value function between men, women, and non-binary persons.
It allows intersectional extensions (e.g., Gender x Age x Culture).
It operationalizes empirically demonstrable differences in FEPSDE dimensions.
axioms.text: Men, women, and non-binary persons have on average different utility structures. These differences can be biologically, socially, or culturally shaped. Gender differentiation allows more precise simulation of behavioral patterns.

variables.U_{d,gender}(t): Utility in dimension d for gender group at time t

axioms.title: Cultural & Institutional Contexts
scope: This axiom describes the influence of culture and institutions on individual value.
It allows representation of national, regional, and local differences.
It integrates institutional stability, norms, and values.
axioms.text: Culture and institutions shape the perception of utility and disutility. What is valuable in one context can be worthless or even negative in another. This axiom operationalizes the dependence of individual value on cultural and institutional framework conditions.

variables.U_d(t): Utility in dimension d at time t

axioms.title: Digital Utility Axis
scope: This axiom defines digitality as an independent utility axis.
It allows representation of utility and disutility related to digital technologies and environments.
It supplements the classical dimensions (financial, emotional, psychological, social, ecological).
axioms.text: Digitalization has created an independent utility axis. Individual value can be strongly influenced by digital aspects such as privacy, connectivity, reputation, and digital identity.

axioms.title: Habit Dampening
scope: This axiom describes the influence of habits on individual value.
It applies universally in all dimensions.
It allows modeling of stability and path dependence.
axioms.text: The more strongly an action is habitualized, the weaker new gains or pains have effect. Habits dampen the effect of changes and make behavior more inert. This axiom explains path dependencies and the difficulty of changing routines.

variables.U_d(t): Utility in dimension d at time t

axioms.title: Intersectionality
scope: This axiom describes that individual value functions cannot be understood in isolation by one segment (e.g., gender or age).
It allows simultaneous consideration of multiple affiliations and their overlaps.
It operationalizes empirical observations on intersectionality.
axioms.text: Individual value often results not from one affiliation alone but from the overlap of multiple dimensions such as gender, age, socioeconomic status, culture, or ethnicity. Intersectionality explains why some groups show particular vulnerability or resilience.
axioms.formula: U_d(t) = f(Gender, Age, SES, Ethnicity, Culture, Institutions)

axioms.title: Stress & Emotional Regulation
scope: This axiom describes the influence of stress on individual value.
It integrates coping mechanisms and resilience.
It applies universally in all FEPSDE dimensions.
axioms.text: Stress reduces individual value. Emotional regulation, coping strategies, and resilience act as buffers. This axiom explains why the same situation means hardly any value loss for some people while others suffer greatly.

axioms.title: Social Comparison Dynamics
scope: This axiom describes the significance of social comparisons for individual value.
It integrates relative and absolute reference points.
It applies particularly in financial, social, and digital dimensions.
axioms.text: People evaluate their value not absolutely but relative to peers. Comparison with others can increase utility (status gains) or create pain (status losses). Social comparison dynamics explain why inequality can have negative effects even with objective prosperity.

axioms.title: Technological Disruption
scope: This axiom describes the influence of technological leaps on individual value.
It allows representation of sudden, discontinuous changes.
It is particularly relevant for digital and ecological dimensions.
axioms.text: Technological shocks change value structures abruptly. They can create short-term pain (e.g., job loss) but also large long-term gains (e.g., productivity, health). This axiom explains the non-linear effect of innovation.
axioms.formula: U_d(t+1) = U_d(t) + Δ_disruption(t), Δ_disruption(t) = Shock(t) * σ_d

axioms.title: Collateral Damage
scope: This axiom describes unintended negative side effects of actions and interventions.
It allows systematic integration of second-order effects.
It applies universally in all FEPSDE dimensions.
axioms.text: Every action can create unintended negative side effects. Collateral Damage describes these harmful effects that often occur in different dimensions than the intended gains.

variables.CD(a,t): Collateral Damage from action a at time t
variables.φ_d^-: Weight of negative side effects in dimension d

axioms.title: Collateral Beauty
scope: This axiom describes unintended positive side effects of actions and interventions.
It complements Collateral Damage and allows a balanced consideration.
It applies universally in all FEPSDE dimensions.
axioms.text: Every action can create unintended positive side effects. Collateral Beauty describes these positive effects that become visible in different dimensions than the original intention.

variables.CB(a,t): Collateral Beauty from action a at time t
variables.φ_d^+: Weight of positive side effects in dimension d
variables.SideEffect_d(a,t): Positive side effect in dimension d

axioms.title: Reaction Time Simulation (Time Will Tell Integration)
axioms.text: The reaction time of a decision is an endogenous function of preference clarity (ΔV), individual base speed (RT_i), item difficulty (RT_j), and stochastic noise factors. The stronger the difference in perceived value between two options, the faster the decision; the smaller the difference, the longer the decision takes.
axioms.formula: RT_{i,j} = RT_i * RT_j * (1 / (1 + α * ΔV)) + ε

variables.RT_{i,j}: Simulated reaction time for person i and task j
variables.RT_i: Individual base reaction speed (person characteristic, e.g., from calibration)
variables.RT_j: Item-specific base time (depends on question complexity, length, cognitive load)
variables.α: Sensitivity parameter controlling speed of reaction time change depending on ΔV
variables.ε: Stochastic component (noise, e.g., normal distribution N(0,σ²))

integration: Context Module 8904 (for item difficulty and information load)

axioms.title: Preference Reconstruction Under Noise
scope: This axiom applies to all contexts where decisions are error-prone (noisy).
It operationalizes the insight that preferences are only indirectly observable.
axioms.text: Individual preferences are latent and not directly observable. Decisions contain noise, which is why single choices are not sufficient to reconstruct stable preferences. By combining choice frequencies and process data such as reaction times, preferences can be estimated more reliably.

variables.ΔU(x,y): Utility difference between option x and y
variables.RT(x,y): Reaction time for decision between x and y
variables.p(x|y): Probability that x is chosen over y

axioms.title: Item-Corrected Relative Reaction Time
axioms.text: The reaction time of a decision is only informative for preference strength when corrected for individual baseline speed and item-specific difficulty. This distinguishes between cognitive processing load and decision certainty.

variables.RT_{i,j}: Response time of person i for decision j
variables.RT̄_i: Average response time of person i across all items
variables.BaselineRT_j: Difficulty of item j, measured by average response time of all persons or other complexity measures

interpretation.RelRT < 1: Decision faster than expected → clear preference
interpretation.RelRT > 1: Decision slower than expected → uncertain preference

axioms.derivation: Based on Fehr et al., 'Time Will Tell' (2022). Links choice data with reaction time and item difficulty to precisely reconstruct latent preferences even under noise.

axioms.title: Emotional Valence (Pride, Shame, Guilt)
axioms.text: Emotions like pride, shame, or guilt modulate the perception of gains and pains beyond the hot-vs-cold state. They act as amplifiers or dampeners on the individual value function.
axioms.formula: U_emotion(a,t) = ε_pride * Pride - ε_shame * Shame - ε_guilt * Guilt

axioms.title: Systemic Feedback Loops
axioms.text: Individual behavior changes context in the long term, whereby the individual value function is endogenously influenced. Behavior is thus not only an outcome but also input for future framework conditions.

variables.Behavior_i: Aggregated behavior of actors in the system
variables.Context: Economic, social, political, and institutional framework conditions

axioms.title: Bounded Attention
axioms.text: Individuals can only process a subset of relevant information simultaneously. This limits the effective weighting of individual dimensions in the value function.

variables.AttentionShare(d,t): Share of cognitive resources allocated to dimension

axioms.title: Self-Control Conflicts
axioms.text: Individuals have time inconsistencies between the long-term planning self (long-run self) and the short-term acting self (short-run self).

axioms.title: Spillover Effects
axioms.text: A behavior or decision in one domain positively or negatively affects utility in other domains. Spillover effects are central to multi-dimensional decisions.

variables.Spillover(d→j,t): Transfer effect from domain d to domain j

axioms.title: Physiological Basic Needs as Foundation
scope: This axiom applies universally to all individual value functions.
It ensures that individual utility in all FEPSDE dimensions is only relevant above a minimum.
It operationalizes the dependence of behavior and decisions on satisfying basic physiological needs.
axioms.text: The individual value function is hierarchically structured. Without a minimum level of physiological satisfaction (e.g., food, water, sleep, physical safety), higher utility components lose relevance or cannot be activated at all. This foundation acts as a constraint for all other utility components.
axioms.formula: U_total(t) = f(BasePhysNeeds(t)) * Σ_d U_d(t), with f(BasePhysNeeds) ∈ [0,1]

variables.BasePhysNeeds(t): Fulfillment level of physiological basic needs at time t
variables.U_d(t): Utility in dimension d (FEPSDE) at time t
variables.f(BasePhysNeeds): Scaling function that only releases utility when minimum level of physiological needs is met

interpretation.BasePhysNeeds < threshold: All higher utility values (e.g., social, identity) are reduced or blocked
interpretation.BasePhysNeeds ≥ threshold: Higher utility values unfold their full effect

axioms.title: Bias Corrections (Cognitive Biases)
scope: This axiom applies to all individual value functions and decision processes.
It operationalizes how systematic cognitive biases distort the evaluation of utility and disutility.
It is universally applicable but varies in strength by culture and segment.
axioms.text: Individuals systematically deviate from rational evaluations because they are subject to cognitive biases (e.g., status quo bias, framing effects, overconfidence, anchoring). These biases change the weighting of gain and pain and act like transformations on the value function.

variables.U_d(t): Utility in dimension d (FEPSDE) at time t
variables.θ_bias,d: Bias coefficient per dimension d; models strength and direction of bias effect

interpretation.θ_bias,d > 0: Bias leads to overestimation of utility (e.g., overconfidence)
interpretation.θ_bias,d < 0: Bias leads to underestimation of utility (e.g., loss aversion overweighting)

axioms.title: Moral Preferences (Altruism, Revenge, Reciprocity)
scope: This axiom applies to all individual value functions shaped by moral considerations.
It operationalizes utility that arises not from individual gain but from morally charged interactions.
It integrates altruism (benefiting others), revenge (harming others), and reciprocity (response behavior to fairness or unfairness).
axioms.text: Besides individual, collective, and identity utility, values arise from moral preferences. Individuals experience positive utility when helping others (altruism) or restoring fairness (reciprocity), and can also derive utility from punishing unfair behavior (revenge). Moral preferences operate strongly context- and segment-specifically and can explain actions against immediate self-interest.
axioms.formula: U_moral(t) = ε_altruism * U_other_gain - ε_spite * U_other_gain + ε_recip * f(Fairness_dev)

variables.ε_spite: Sensitivity for envy- or revenge-driven preferences
variables.U_other_gain: Perceived utility/disutility of another person or group

interpretation.ε_spite > 0: Joy in harming others (e.g., revenge, envy)
interpretation.ε_recip > 0: Joy in fairness restoration (reward or punishment)

axioms.title: Intertemporal Identity Investment
scope: This axiom applies to all individual value functions concerning investments in the future self.
It operationalizes that individuals derive utility from actions that shape their identity or self-image long-term.
It explains behavior such as education, training, religious asceticism, or sustainable consumption.
axioms.text: Individuals evaluate actions not only by immediate gain but also by how strongly they contribute to long-term identity formation. Decisions act as investments in the future self and create utility through congruence with a desired self-image (e.g., 'I am a disciplined person').
axioms.formula: U_ID(t) = β_ID * Σ_{τ>t} δ^{τ-t} * Consistency(Self_future(τ), Action(t))

variables.U_ID(t): Utility from identity investment at time t
variables.δ: Discount factor for future time points
variables.Self_future(τ): Expected future self-image at time τ
variables.Consistency: Function measuring how strongly an action aligns with future self-image

interpretation.U_ID(t) high: Action fits desired self-image and creates long-term utility

axioms.title: Self-Uncertainty (Noisy Preferences)
scope: This axiom applies to all individual utility functions where preferences are unstable or hard to observe.
It operationalizes that preferences are not fixed but fluctuating and overlaid by uncertainty.
It considers both internal uncertainty (self-doubt, fluctuating identity) and external uncertainty (complex choice environments).
axioms.text: Individual preferences are not stable fixed points but are influenced by uncertainty, cognitive limitations, and stochastic processes. Decisions can therefore appear inconsistent even when based on the same preference system. Reaction times, choice probabilities, and context factors must be combined to reconstruct preferences.

variables.U_total(t): Observed utility of a decision at time t
variables.ε_pref: Noise component (e.g., normal distribution N(0,σ²) or logit error)

interpretation.Small ε_pref: Preferences are stable and consistently observable
interpretation.Large ε_pref: Preferences appear erratic and hard to reconstruct
interpretation.Persistent ε_pref: Systematic distortions, e.g., self-doubt, changing identities

axioms.title: Digital Amplification (Social Media Reinforcement)
scope: This axiom applies to all contexts where digital platforms and algorithms amplify individual preferences, emotions, and behavior.
It operationalizes the influence of social media, algorithmic nudging, recommendation logic, and filter bubbles on individual utility function.
It considers that digital feedback loops work faster, more intensively, and more globally than analog interactions.
axioms.text: Digital systems amplify emotions, preferences, and identity markers through algorithmic selection and feedback loops. Likes, shares, and algorithmically personalized content cause small differences in preferences or emotions to be disproportionately amplified. This changes salience, perceived reference points, and weighting of individual utility dimensions (especially social, emotional, digital).

variables.U_digital(t): Individual digital utility at time t
variables.Feedback(t): Aggregated feedback (likes, shares, comments, algorithmic reactions)

interpretation.High Feedback values: Strong polarization and potential overshooting of preferences

axioms.title: Path Dependence & Irreversibility
scope: This axiom applies to all individual value functions shaped by past actions and decisions.
It operationalizes the effect that earlier decisions change, limit, or expand future options.
It considers that some behavioral consequences are irreversible and permanently shift the reference point.
axioms.text: Individual decisions are not isolated but have long-term feedback effects on one's own utility function. Path dependencies arise when a once-chosen option systematically influences the probability of future options. Irreversibility occurs when certain decisions (e.g., addiction, education, migration, investments, digital traces) permanently change the value function and block alternative paths.
axioms.formula: U_total(t+1) = U_total(t) + φ_path * PastChoices(t) - φ_irrev * LostOptions(t)

variables.LostOptions(t): Number or value of lost action options

interpretation.High φ_path: Strong reinforcement through habits, routines, or lock-in effects
interpretation.High φ_irrev: Loss of options has permanently negative effect
interpretation.Combination: A behavior can create positive paths (e.g., education) or negative lock-ins (e.g., addiction)

axioms.title: Meta-Cognition (Self-Evaluation)
scope: This axiom applies to all individual value functions that consider self-reflection, self-control, and self-evaluation.
It operationalizes that people derive utility not only from actions but also from their own evaluation of these actions.
It explains phenomena such as pride, shame, guilt, cognitive dissonance, or the feeling of moral coherence.
axioms.text: Individuals observe their own actions and reconstruct a self-image from them. Depending on whether action and self-image are consistent or inconsistent, additional utility (pride, self-affirmation) or disutility (shame, guilt, dissonance) arises. Meta-cognition is thus a recursive process: actions influence self-image, and self-image influences future actions.
axioms.formula: U_meta(t) = η_pos * Consistency(Self(t), Action(t)) - η_neg * Inconsistency(Self(t), Action(t))

variables.Consistency: Degree of alignment between action and self-image
variables.Inconsistency: Degree of deviation between action and self-image
variables.η_neg: Sensitivity for negative self-evaluation (e.g., guilt, shame)

interpretation.U_meta high: Actions and self-image are consistent, create pride or self-affirmation
interpretation.U_meta low: Actions contradict self-image, create guilt or shame
interpretation.Long-term: Meta-cognition stabilizes or changes self-image through repeated cycles

axioms.title: Physical Complementarity
axioms.text: The physical dimension (health, energy, pain, vitality) acts as a multiplicative base effect on all other utility axes. Deficits reduce, surplus amplifies the effective utility of other dimensions.
axioms.formula: U_d_eff(t) = U_d(t) * φ_phys(Health(t)), d ∈ {fin, emo, phy, soc, dig, eco}

variables.U_d(t): Utility in dimension d at time t
variables.φ_phys(Health(t)): Multiplicative factor depending on physical health/energy

axioms.title: Social Media Addiction (Digital Addiction)
scope: This axiom applies to all individual value functions that represent digital usage and platform dependence.
It operationalizes the mechanism that feedback loops in social media (likes, notifications, dopamine peaks) lead to disproportionate digital utility.
It explains escalating usage intensities and self-reinforcement despite negative side effects.
axioms.text: Social media and digital platforms are designed to activate addiction mechanisms. Repeated usage reinforces short-term emotional and social utility but can simultaneously create long-term ecological, social, and psychological disutility. This dynamic leads to endogenous reinforcement of digital utility with simultaneous increase of pain in other dimensions.
axioms.formula: U_digital(t+1) = U_digital(t) + α_add * Reward(t) - β_cost * Spillover(t)

variables.Spillover(t): Negative spillover to other dimensions (e.g., sleep, work, relationships)

interpretation.High α_add, low β_cost: Digital addiction spiral, hardly perceived costs
interpretation.High β_cost: Perception of negative consequences, possible regulation
interpretation.Long-term: Stable distortion of preference structure toward digital salience

axioms.title: Financial ↔ Emotional Complementarity
axioms.text: Financial utility unfolds more strongly when it also creates emotional security or joy (e.g., gift vs. money). Conversely, emotional stress amplifies the negative effects of financial losses.

axioms.title: Financial ↔ Psychological Complementarity
axioms.text: Financial reward works more strongly when it strengthens psychological self-efficacy. Financial losses weigh more heavily when psychologically associated with failure.

axioms.title: Financial ↔ Social Complementarity
axioms.text: Money often has social value (status, recognition, participation). A financial gain amplifies social utility, a loss weakens it.

axioms.title: Financial ↔ Digital Complementarity
axioms.text: Digital goods and infrastructures gain value when financially accessible. Financial gains can enable digital self-actualization.

axioms.title: Financial ↔ Ecological Complementarity
axioms.text: Sustainable investments have high value when financially viable. Financial gains increase the scope for ecologically motivated decisions.

axioms.title: Emotional ↔ Psychological Complementarity
axioms.text: Emotional states are closely linked to psychological self-perception. Joy strengthens self-efficacy, stress weakens it.

axioms.title: Emotional ↔ Social Complementarity
axioms.text: Emotional experiences are often socially shaped. Joy or shame unfold more strongly in social contexts.

axioms.title: Emotional ↔ Digital Complementarity
axioms.text: Digital interactions can trigger strong emotional reactions (likes, shitstorms). Emotions amplify the value of digital experiences.

axioms.title: Emotional ↔ Ecological Complementarity
axioms.text: Emotional bonds (e.g., climate shame or pride in sustainable action) amplify the effect of ecological decisions.

axioms.title: Psychological ↔ Social Complementarity
axioms.text: Psychological self-efficacy is reinforced through social recognition. Lack of social feedback can diminish psychological utility.

axioms.title: Psychological ↔ Digital Complementarity
axioms.text: Digital competencies unfold value when psychologically perceived as self-efficacy.

axioms.title: Psychological ↔ Ecological Complementarity
axioms.text: Sustainable behavior can create psychological meaningfulness. Lack of ecological responsibility can amplify psychological dissonance.

axioms.title: Social ↔ Digital Complementarity
axioms.text: Digital platforms unfold value primarily through social interactions (e.g., social media).

axioms.title: Social ↔ Ecological Complementarity
axioms.text: Social recognition amplifies ecologically motivated decisions. Ecological responsibility unfolds social status value.

axioms.title: Digital ↔ Ecological Complementarity
axioms.text: Digital technologies can amplify ecological utility (e.g., through efficiency gains) or weaken it (e.g., energy consumption).
